lesson.title: Rhetorical questions
lesson.text: Hard writers often use questions to express views: "But is this really conservation?", "Who, then, will care for these animals?". A rhetorical question usually implies a doubt or a negative answer. Translate it into a statement, for example: "This is not really conservation." Then compare. Be careful, though: a genuine open question that the writer leaves unanswered does not express a view, so statements about it may be NOT GIVEN.
lesson.example:
Passage: "Can a museum without visitors really be said to serve the public?"
Statement: "A museum without visitors does not truly serve the public." → YES.

questions.q: The arguments in favour of de-extinction should be dismissed as foolish.
questions.evidence: These arguments are not foolish, and I do not wish to dismiss them
questions.explanation: This is a direct contradiction.

questions.q: An animal produced by de-extinction would not be identical to the original species.
questions.evidence: The animals produced would not be mammoths but modified elephants ... Is an animal that looks like a mammoth ... really a restored species?
questions.explanation: The rhetorical question implies "no", which supports the statement.

questions.q: Whether recreated animals are truly the original species is only a philosophical question.
questions.evidence: The question is not merely philosophical; it affects whether such animals could perform the ecological roles
questions.explanation: This contradicts "only".

questions.q: The potential benefit of the technology for living endangered species is the strongest argument for the research.
questions.evidence: The second point strikes me as the strongest argument in favour of the research
questions.explanation: "The second point" refers to helping endangered species, so you must resolve this reference to answer.

questions.q: The claim that de-extinction donors would not otherwise fund conservation is easy to confirm.
questions.evidence: "The first is harder to verify" (Paragraph D), where "the first" is the supporters' claim about private donors.
questions.explanation: "Harder to verify" contradicts "easy to confirm". To answer, you must identify which of the two points "the first" refers to.

questions.q: The mammoth project will be completed within the next decade.
questions.evidence: The writer says the technology is "slow, expensive and uncertain" (Paragraph E) but gives no timeline.
questions.explanation: No prediction is made.

questions.q: It is unrealistic to think that belief in de-extinction could weaken efforts to prevent extinction.
questions.evidence: it would be naive to assume it has no basis
questions.explanation: The writer thinks the fear has some basis, which contradicts "unrealistic to think".

questions.q: Media reports about de-extinction sometimes overstate what has been achieved.
questions.evidence: announcements about de-extinction projects are often reported in terms that exaggerate what has been achieved
questions.explanation: "Often" includes "sometimes", and "exaggerate" = "overstate".

questions.q: De-extinction research should be stopped.
questions.evidence: None of this means that the research should be abandoned
questions.explanation: This is a direct contradiction.

lesson.title: Criticism of a framing, not the thing itself
lesson.text:
Some writers criticise how an idea is presented or pursued rather than the idea itself. A writer may support using data to improve cities while criticising the "smart city" slogan. Statements then test the difference:

"Data can help cities" → YES.

"Cities should avoid technology" → NO.

"The smart city label misrepresents priorities" → YES.

Ask: Is the writer against the thing, or against a particular way of thinking about it?

questions.q: Using data to improve urban services is acceptable in principle.
questions.evidence: I have no quarrel with the use of data to improve urban services
questions.explanation: This is a double negative meaning "I accept it".

questions.q: Smart-city projects often start from technology rather than from existing problems.
questions.evidence: Much smart-city thinking begins with the technology and then looks for problems it might solve
questions.explanation: "Much" supports "often".

questions.q: Housing costs can be solved mainly through technical innovation.
questions.evidence: not primarily technical ... A sensor network cannot make housing affordable
questions.explanation: This is a direct contradiction.

questions.q: Small, targeted data projects have produced demonstrable benefits.
questions.evidence: have achieved real improvements ... their benefits are easier to demonstrate
questions.explanation: This matches "demonstrable benefits".

questions.q: Most new technology-based cities have met their population targets.
questions.evidence: "Several have attracted far fewer residents than planned" and "on the whole, had a disappointing record"
questions.explanation: The writer's judgement contradicts "most have met".

questions.q: Technology companies deliberately designed the new cities to fail.
questions.evidence: The writer attributes failure to cities being designed "around its infrastructure rather than its inhabitants" (Paragraph D) and never suggests any intention to fail.
questions.explanation: No view on deliberate intent is expressed. This is a trap for students who read criticism as an accusation.

questions.q: Data collection in cities should be abandoned because of privacy risks.
questions.evidence: These are not reasons to reject data collection outright
questions.explanation: This is a direct contradiction.

questions.q: Critics of smart cities are opposed to progress.
questions.evidence: That is a misunderstanding
questions.explanation: The writer rejects this characterisation of critics.

questions.q: Cities should consult residents before choosing technological solutions.
questions.evidence: A wise city would begin by asking its residents ... and only then consider which tools
questions.explanation: This matches the order in the statement.

lesson.title: Counter-intuitive arguments
lesson.text: Some writers argue against a common assumption: "More testing is always better", "Early detection always saves lives". Statements may present the common assumption as if the writer held it. Before answering, write the common assumption and the writer's correction side by side. Also check for the writer's limits: arguing that screening can cause harm is not the same as arguing that screening should be abolished.

questions.q: Some screening programmes have prevented many deaths.
questions.evidence: some have undoubtedly prevented many deaths
questions.explanation: "Undoubtedly" shows that the writer accepts this.

questions.q: The claim that early detection saves lives is misleading when stated without qualification.
questions.evidence: Yet the principle, stated so simply, is misleading
questions.explanation: "Stated so simply" = "without qualification".

questions.q: False alarms are an insignificant problem when considered across a whole population.
questions.evidence: Across a whole population, it is a substantial one
questions.explanation: This is a direct contradiction.

questions.q: Doctors can usually identify which early abnormalities will progress to serious disease.
questions.evidence: doctors cannot reliably tell which cases would have progressed
questions.explanation: This is a direct contradiction.

questions.q: Patients who have been overdiagnosed usually realise that their treatment was unnecessary.
questions.evidence: these patients typically believe that screening saved their lives
questions.explanation: This is the opposite of realising the treatment was unnecessary.

questions.q: Researchers agree on precise rates of overdiagnosis for most diseases.
questions.evidence: Estimates vary widely ... researchers disagree about particular figures
questions.explanation: This contradicts "agree on precise rates".

questions.q: Screening programmes in general should be abolished.
questions.evidence: None of this is an argument against screening as such ... I would encourage people in those groups to take part
questions.explanation: This is a direct contradiction.

questions.q: Private whole-body scans are more expensive than public screening programmes.
questions.evidence: Private scans are criticised for leading to unnecessary treatment (Paragraph E). Their price is never mentioned.
questions.explanation: No view on cost is expressed.

questions.q: People should be free to decline screening once properly informed.
questions.evidence: some decide not to. That seems to me exactly as it should be. The decision belongs to the individual
questions.explanation: This matches the writer's view.

lesson.title: Final review — the full YNNG method
lesson.text:
This final set combines the main YNNG skills: concessions, double negatives, rhetorical questions, conditional views, reported views and the difference between NO and NOT GIVEN. For each statement:

1. Find the section and decide whose voice it is.

2. Translate complex phrasing into a plain view.

3. Compare the statement's claim and strength with the writer's view.

4. If the writer never takes a position on that exact claim, the answer is NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: Rating systems have in many ways delivered what they promised.
questions.evidence: In many respects, the promise has been fulfilled
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: A three-star rating is generally understood by customers as a serious criticism.
questions.evidence: A customer who gives three stars may think they are indicating 'satisfactory' when they are, in effect, delivering a severe penalty
questions.explanation: The writer says customers intend three stars as satisfactory, which contradicts "understood by customers as a serious criticism". The penalty is its effect, not the customers' understanding.

questions.q: It is fair for workers' jobs to depend on unclear rating scales.
questions.evidence: Is it reasonable that someone's job should depend on how strangers interpret a scale that was never clearly defined?
questions.explanation: The rhetorical question implies "no".

questions.q: Customer satisfaction is not a reliable measure of quality in every case.
questions.evidence: Ratings ... measure satisfaction, which is not the same as quality
questions.explanation: This matches the statement.

questions.q: Satisfaction is of no importance.
questions.evidence: it would be wrong to conclude that satisfaction is unimportant
questions.explanation: This is a direct contradiction.

questions.q: Measures to detect fake reviews have completely solved the problem.
questions.evidence: with some success, but the problem has not disappeared
questions.explanation: This contradicts "completely solved".

questions.q: Rating systems have given consumers real influence over businesses.
questions.evidence: they have given consumers genuine power ... This is not a trivial achievement
questions.explanation: The writer accepts the defenders' point.

questions.q: Ratings of hotels are more reliable than ratings of restaurants.
questions.evidence: Hotels and restaurants appear only in a list in Paragraph A.
questions.explanation: The writer never compares the reliability of ratings in different sectors.

questions.q: Younger consumers rely on online ratings more than older consumers.
questions.evidence: Age groups are not mentioned.
questions.explanation: No view is expressed.

lesson.title: Use names, dates and numbers first
lesson.text: In an easy Matching Information set, several questions contain or imply a specific detail: a date, an inventor, a number, or a distinctive object. Answer those first, because they are fastest to find. Then use the paragraphs you have not yet used to help locate the harder items. Remember that one paragraph can contain two answers.
lesson.example: Question: "the name of a person who improved the design". Scan for capital letters (names) and read the sentence around each one.

questions.q: an explanation of why front wheels became larger
questions.evidence: each turn of the pedals moved the machine forward by exactly one turn of the wheel. To travel faster, designers made the front wheel larger.
questions.explanation: This is the explanation (cause → effect). Note that C is used twice in this set.

questions.q: a reference to restrictions on where early machines could be ridden
questions.evidence: Complaints from pedestrians led some cities to ban the machines from pavements.
questions.explanation: "Ban from pavements" = "restrictions on where machines could be ridden".

questions.q: the reason why one type of machine received an unflattering nickname
questions.evidence: they gave such an uncomfortable ride that they earned the nickname 'boneshakers'.
questions.explanation: The uncomfortable ride is the reason for the name. Paragraph C also mentions a nickname ("penny-farthing"), but it gives a different reason (coin sizes), and that name is not unflattering.

questions.q: a description of how a chain made it possible to build a lower, fast machine
questions.evidence: the chain allowed a small wheel to turn quickly, so that the machine could be fast without being tall.
questions.explanation: "Without being tall" = "lower".

questions.q: a mention of the effect of cycling on what people wore
questions.evidence: It also encouraged changes in women's clothing.
questions.explanation: "Clothing" = "what people wore".

questions.q: a claim about why a new type of tyre was first invented
questions.evidence: reportedly to make his young son's tricycle more comfortable.
questions.explanation: "Reportedly" matches "a claim".

questions.q: a reference to machines that use electrical power
questions.evidence: electric bicycles have made cycling practical for longer distances.
questions.explanation: "Electric" = "electrical power".

questions.q: a description of a risk faced by riders of one type of machine
questions.evidence: if the front wheel struck an obstacle, they could be thrown forward over the handlebars.
questions.explanation: This describes the risk of riding a high-wheeler.

lesson.title: Work paragraph by paragraph
lesson.text: With a short, well-organised passage, an efficient method is to read one paragraph at a time and then look down the full list of questions to see which items that paragraph answers. This is often faster than taking each question and searching the whole passage. Mark each question as soon as you answer it, so that you don't read it again.
lesson.example: After reading a paragraph about an animal's eyes, check the question list for anything involving sight, vision, seeing, eyes, light.

questions.q: an explanation of how owls avoid injury when turning their heads
questions.evidence: Special features of the bones and blood vessels ... allow them to do so without cutting off the supply of blood to the brain.
questions.explanation: This explains how injury is avoided.

questions.q: a reference to a practical use of owl research outside biology
questions.evidence: Engineers have studied these features in the hope of designing quieter aircraft and wind turbines.
questions.explanation: Aircraft design is a use outside biology.

questions.q: a description of how owls judge the vertical position of a sound
questions.evidence: ear openings are positioned at different heights ... allowing the owl to judge ... the height of its source.
questions.explanation: "Height" = "vertical position".

questions.q: the number of owl species
questions.evidence: Of the roughly two hundred and fifty species.
questions.explanation: This is the only number of species given in the passage.

questions.q: a reason why owls must turn their heads to look around
questions.evidence: the eyes cannot move within their sockets. To look in a different direction, an owl must turn its whole head.
questions.explanation: Paragraph C describes how the head turns, but the reason it must turn is in B. This is a similar-detail trap.

questions.q: a method of studying small animals without catching them
questions.evidence: researchers can ... learn about the populations of small mammals in an area without having to trap them.
questions.explanation: "Without having to trap" = "without catching".

questions.q: measures that have helped some owl populations
questions.evidence: the provision of nest boxes and the protection of grassland ... have helped owl numbers recover.
questions.explanation: This matches "measures that have helped".

questions.q: evidence that some owls can hunt without using their eyes
questions.evidence: barn owls can catch mice in complete darkness, guided by sound alone.
questions.explanation: "Guided by sound alone" means without sight. D is used twice.

lesson.title: Dates as signposts
lesson.text: Historical passages usually move forward in time. If a question mentions or implies a period ("the earliest", "in the nineteenth century", "today"), use the dates in the passage to jump to the right paragraph. But be careful: a paragraph may mention a date only in passing, and the information asked for may be in a neighbouring paragraph.
lesson.example: Question: "a reference to a change in the eighteenth century". Scan for 17-- dates, then read the whole sentence to check that it describes a change.

questions.q: a reference to cacao being used as currency
questions.evidence: the beans ... were used as a form of money.
questions.explanation: "Money" = "currency".

questions.q: an explanation of why chocolate remained costly in Europe for a long time
questions.evidence: Because cacao had to be imported from distant plantations, it remained an expensive luxury.
questions.explanation: The paragraph gives the reason with "because".

questions.q: the name of a person who helped another inventor by supplying an ingredient
questions.evidence: He used a form of condensed milk developed by his neighbour, Henri Nestlé.
questions.explanation: Nestlé supplied the ingredient that Peter needed.

questions.q: a description of where the pods grow on the tree
questions.evidence: pods that sprout directly from the trunk and branches.
questions.explanation: This describes where the pods grow.

questions.q: a process that made chocolate less bitter
questions.evidence: treated the powder with alkaline salts to reduce its bitterness.
questions.explanation: Paragraph C also mentions sweetening with sugar, but that improved the taste rather than removing bitterness through a process. D describes a specific process for reducing bitterness.

questions.q: a reference to places where people met to discuss business
questions.evidence: chocolate houses ... where customers gathered to drink chocolate and discuss business.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match. C is used twice in this set.

questions.q: doubts about schemes intended to help cacao farmers
questions.evidence: their effectiveness is debated.
questions.explanation: "Debated" = "doubts".

questions.q: a farming method that may help protect the crop
questions.evidence: growing cacao among other trees, which provide shade and may help protect the crop.
questions.explanation: This matches the statement, including "may".

lesson.title: Cause and effect in scientific passages
lesson.text: Many questions ask for "an explanation of" or "a cause of". In scientific passages, one paragraph may describe what happens and another may explain why. Look for cause words (because, as a result, this means, which causes, due to) and make sure the paragraph you choose contains the explanation, not just a description or example.
lesson.example: Question: "an explanation of why the coast is dry". A paragraph that simply says "the coast receives little rain" describes the fact but does not explain it. Look for the paragraph that gives the reason.

questions.q: an explanation of why sinking air prevents clouds forming
questions.evidence: As it sinks, it becomes warmer and even drier, preventing clouds from forming.
questions.explanation: This is the explanation.

questions.q: a definition of a desert based on rainfall
questions.evidence: a region that receives less than 250 millimetres of rain a year.
questions.explanation: This is a definition based on rainfall.

questions.q: a reference to efforts to stop sand moving
questions.evidence: methods of slowing their movement, such as planting vegetation and building barriers.
questions.explanation: This matches "efforts to stop sand moving".

questions.q: an explanation of how a sea current contributes to dryness
questions.evidence: a cold ocean current ... cooling the air above it. Cool air holds less moisture and does not rise easily.
questions.explanation: This gives the cause-and-effect explanation.

questions.q: an example of a desert with very cold winters
questions.evidence: the Gobi experiences very cold winters.
questions.explanation: Antarctica (F) is cold all year round, but the question specifies cold winters, which matches the description of the Gobi.

questions.q: a description of what happens to air on the downwind side of mountains
questions.evidence: descends on the other side, it has lost most of its moisture.
questions.explanation: "Other side" = "downwind side".

questions.q: the proportion of deserts covered by sand dunes
questions.evidence: cover only around a fifth of the world's desert areas.
questions.explanation: "A fifth" is a proportion. Paragraph A mentions "a third", but that is the proportion of land covered by deserts, not the proportion of deserts covered by dunes.

questions.q: a reason why snow builds up in polar deserts
questions.evidence: accumulates over long periods because it rarely melts.
questions.explanation: This gives the reason.

lesson.title: "Firsts" and "problems"
lesson.text: Two very common question types in history passages are "the first..." and "a problem with...". For "first" questions, check that the passage really presents something as the first (earliest, first, the original, before any other). For "problem" questions, look for negative language (difficulty, danger, failed, exploded, was expensive). Both may appear in several paragraphs, so read each candidate sentence carefully.
lesson.example: Question: "a problem with an early design". Candidate sentence: "The first model worked well but was expensive to produce." The problem is cost, even though the design "worked well".

questions.q: a reference to an accident involving an early signal
questions.evidence: the gas lamp exploded, injuring the police officer operating it.
questions.explanation: This describes the accident.

questions.q: a reason why police officers directing traffic were at a disadvantage
questions.evidence: Police officers directing traffic ... were exposed to danger and bad weather, and they could not always be seen clearly.
questions.explanation: This matches "at a disadvantage".

questions.q: a description of a signal that used sound to warn drivers
questions.evidence: a buzzer to warn drivers that the lights were about to change.
questions.explanation: "Buzzer" = "sound". C is used twice in this set.

questions.q: a mention of an inventor who chose not to protect his design legally
questions.evidence: Potts ... did not patent his design.
questions.explanation: Patenting protects a design legally. Morgan (E) did patent his design, which makes E a trap.

questions.q: a problem with signals that changed at regular intervals
questions.evidence: changing at the same intervals regardless of how much traffic was waiting. This was inefficient.
questions.explanation: "Same intervals" = "regular intervals".

questions.q: features that help people who cannot see well
questions.evidence: sounds or vibrating panels that help people with visual impairments.
questions.explanation: "Visual impairments" = "cannot see well".

questions.q: a proposal to take away traffic lights in some places
questions.evidence: some planners have argued that ... removing traffic lights altogether ... can make streets safer.
questions.explanation: This matches "a proposal to take away traffic lights in some places".

questions.q: the location of the first ever traffic signal
questions.evidence: The first traffic signal was installed in London ... outside the Houses of Parliament.
questions.explanation: Paragraph C mentions "one of the earliest" electric signals, but only B identifies the very first signal.

lesson.title: Paragraphs that contain more than one answer
lesson.text: Some paragraphs are packed with information, and two or even three questions may point to the same one. Don't avoid a letter just because you have already used it, especially when the instructions say "You may use any letter more than once." On the other hand, some paragraphs may contain no answers at all. Your goal is to match each detail to the correct paragraph, not to use every letter.
lesson.example: If one paragraph mentions both "how long a cycle lasts" and "what happens to the muscles", both questions can have the same answer.

questions.q: the length of a typical sleep cycle
questions.evidence: each lasting roughly ninety minutes.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: a reference to a change in how sleep was understood
questions.evidence: sleep was regarded as a simple state of rest ... That view began to change in the 1950s.
questions.explanation: This describes a change in understanding.

questions.q: a possible reason why the body is still during dreams
questions.evidence: the muscles of the body are almost completely relaxed – which may prevent people from acting out their dreams.
questions.explanation: This gives a possible reason.

questions.q: a suggestion about when schools should begin the day
questions.evidence: this should be taken into account when setting school starting times.
questions.explanation: This matches "when schools should begin".

questions.q: a reference to research that may not apply to humans
questions.evidence: much of the research so far has been carried out on mice, and its relevance to humans is not yet certain.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: evidence that sleep improves the ability to remember
questions.evidence: people who sleep after learning new information remember it better.
questions.explanation: This is the evidence for improved memory.

questions.q: a reason why dreams are more often remembered near waking time
questions.evidence: REM sleep becomes longer in the later ones. This is why a person woken shortly before their usual waking time is more likely to remember a dream.
questions.explanation: C contains two answers in this set.

questions.q: a reference to people underestimating the effects of lack of sleep
questions.evidence: people who are sleep-deprived are often poor judges of how impaired they are.
questions.explanation: "Poor judges" = "underestimating".

lesson.title: Similar details in several paragraphs
lesson.example: Coins appear in paragraphs C and E. Question: "a disadvantage of using metal coins". C describes their invention; E explains that coins were heavy to transport → E.

questions.q: a challenge to a commonly taught explanation
questions.evidence: Economics textbooks have traditionally explained ... Many anthropologists, however, have challenged this account.
questions.explanation: "Traditionally explained" in textbooks = "commonly taught".

questions.q: a reason why people might stop trusting coins
questions.evidence: rulers ... reduce the amount of precious metal ... When people realised this had happened, they often lost confidence in the coins.
questions.explanation: "Lost confidence" = "stop trusting".

questions.q: an example of a technology that helped people without access to banks
questions.evidence: allowed people without bank accounts to store and send money using simple text messages.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: a description of the features that made early coins convenient
questions.evidence: they were durable, easy to count and could be carried ... the stamp of a ruler meant that their value did not have to be tested.
questions.explanation: Coins are also mentioned in D, but D describes their problems.

questions.q: a reference to a system that restricted the amount of money governments could issue
questions.evidence: This system limited how much money governments could create.
questions.explanation: "Limited" = "restricted".

questions.q: the purposes that all forms of money serve
questions.evidence: they are accepted as a means of exchange, a way of measuring value and a way of storing wealth.
questions.explanation: These are the purposes common to all forms of money.

questions.q: a reference to the transport of large sums as a problem
questions.evidence: Large payments in coins were also heavy and difficult to transport safely.
questions.explanation: E also refers to carrying money ("could be carried more easily"), but D is where transport is identified as a problem. E presents paper money as the solution. D is used twice.

questions.q: a consequence of producing too much paper money
questions.evidence: printed notes far faster than the economy grew, causing their value to fall sharply.
questions.explanation: F mentions governments creating money, but the consequence of over-printing paper money appears only in E.

lesson.title: Research findings vs theories vs advice
lesson.example: Question: "a practical technique for reducing delay". A paragraph explaining why people delay is not the answer, even though it is on the same topic.

questions.q: a rejection of the idea that procrastination is caused by laziness
questions.evidence: A common assumption is that procrastinators are simply lazy ... Researchers increasingly reject this explanation.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: a finding about how the brain responds to thoughts of oneself in the future
questions.evidence: patterns of brain activity resemble those that occur when they think about strangers.
questions.explanation: This is a finding from brain imaging.

questions.q: a practical technique involving precise planning of when and where to begin
questions.evidence: a person decides exactly when, where and how they will start.
questions.explanation: This is the practical technique. Paragraph D discusses deadlines, but only as a description of task features, not as advice.

questions.q: the result of a study showing that being kind to oneself can reduce delay
questions.evidence: those who forgave themselves for procrastinating ... procrastinated less.
questions.explanation: "Forgave themselves" = "being kind to oneself".

questions.q: a comparison between the proportions of students and adults who procrastinate
questions.evidence: a substantial minority of adults ... among students the proportion appears to be considerably higher.
questions.explanation: This compares the two proportions.

questions.q: a description of characteristics of tasks that are more often delayed
questions.evidence: People are more likely to delay tasks that are unclear, have distant deadlines or offer rewards only in the long term.
questions.explanation: These are the characteristics of tasks that are delayed.

questions.q: a suggestion that some delay may have benefits
questions.evidence: a certain amount of delay allows ideas to develop.
questions.explanation: This describes a benefit of delay.

questions.q: a link between feeling connected to one's future and financial behaviour
questions.evidence: People who feel more closely connected to their future selves tend to save more money.
questions.explanation: "Save more money" = "financial behaviour". C is used twice.

lesson.title: "A reference to" = a brief mention
lesson.text: When a question says "a reference to" or "a mention of", the information may be very small: a single phrase buried in a paragraph about something else. Don't expect the whole paragraph to be about it. By contrast, "a description of" or "an account of" usually needs a few sentences of detail. Adjust how carefully you scan according to the question's wording.
lesson.example: "A reference to an earthquake" might be satisfied by one clause such as "...which survived the 1906 earthquake..." in a paragraph mainly about building materials.

questions.q: an account of a public demonstration intended to show that a machine was safe
questions.evidence: Standing on a raised platform, he ordered the rope holding it to be cut. Instead of falling, the platform stopped.
questions.explanation: This is the demonstration of safety at an exhibition.

questions.q: a reference to disagreement over which building was the first of its kind
questions.evidence: often cited as the first skyscraper ... though historians debate whether it deserves the title.
questions.explanation: This is only a brief reference: one clause at the end of a sentence. "Debate" = "disagreement".

questions.q: a description of a disaster that led to a demand for new buildings
questions.evidence: A great fire in 1871 had destroyed much of the city centre, creating a demand for rapid rebuilding.
questions.explanation: The fire is the disaster.

questions.q: an explanation of why upper floors eventually became more attractive than lower ones
questions.evidence: eventually more desirable, because they offered light, views and distance from street noise.
questions.explanation: B is used twice. Paragraph A explains why upper floors were unpopular, which is the opposite.

questions.q: a reference to a regulation that changed the appearance of buildings
questions.evidence: regulations requiring buildings ... to step back ... gave many of the city's towers ... their distinctive stepped ... shapes.
questions.explanation: The regulation changed the buildings' appearance.

questions.q: a method of reducing the movement of buildings caused by wind
questions.evidence: installing heavy weights near the top that move in the opposite direction to the building's sway.
questions.explanation: F also mentions shaping the building. Either technique satisfies the question.

questions.q: an example of the space lost because of thick walls
questions.evidence: walls nearly two metres thick at its base, taking up valuable space on the lower floors.
questions.explanation: This is a specific example of lost space.

questions.q: a suggestion that some very tall buildings are built mainly to impress
questions.evidence: many are built more for prestige than for practical necessity.
questions.explanation: "Prestige" = "to impress".

lesson.title: Statistics and proportions
lesson.text: Questions may refer to a statistic without giving the number: "a figure showing how important reefs are for biodiversity". You must find the paragraph whose number fits that purpose. Several paragraphs may contain numbers; check what each number measures.
lesson.example: Question: "a statistic about the economic value of fishing". Paragraph B gives an area in square kilometres; paragraph D gives the number of people employed. D fits "economic", B does not.

questions.q: a figure indicating the importance of reefs for marine life
questions.evidence: occupy less than one per cent of the ocean floor, yet ... support around a quarter of all marine species.
questions.explanation: This figure shows the importance of reefs for marine life. B's figure measures length, which serves a different purpose.

questions.q: a reason why reef-building corals are found mainly in shallow water
questions.evidence: The partnership is also why most reef-building corals are found in shallow, clear, sunlit water.
questions.explanation: The algae need sunlight, which explains the shallow-water location.

questions.q: a comparison between restoring reefs and restoring forests
questions.evidence: rather like replanting a forest.
questions.explanation: A also compares reefs to rainforests, but only for their richness, not for restoration.

questions.q: an explanation of what makes bleached coral appear white
questions.evidence: the coral tissue becomes transparent, revealing the white skeleton beneath.
questions.explanation: This is a direct explanation.

questions.q: a reference to a chemical change in seawater that affects coral growth
questions.evidence: the water becomes slightly more acidic, which makes it harder for corals to build their skeletons.
questions.explanation: "More acidic" = "a chemical change".

questions.q: evidence that protecting reefs from local threats can aid recovery
questions.evidence: Reefs that are protected from local pressures ... often recover more quickly after bleaching.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: a reference to the length of a particular reef system
questions.evidence: stretches for more than two thousand kilometres.
questions.explanation: This is a brief reference to length.

questions.q: a limitation of current restoration projects
questions.evidence: they operate on a very small scale compared with the size of the world's reefs.
questions.explanation: This describes a limitation. F is used twice.

title: The Long Life of the University

lesson.title: Paraphrased time references
lesson.text: Questions rarely repeat exact dates. They may say "a development in the early nineteenth century" when the passage says "in 1810", or "the period after a major war" when the passage says "after 1945". Convert the question's time expression into a rough date range, then scan for dates or time phrases that fall within it.
lesson.example: Question: "a change in the medieval period". Look for dates roughly between 500 and 1500, or phrases such as "in the Middle Ages" or "twelfth century".

questions.q: an explanation of the original meaning of the word "university"
questions.evidence: The Latin word universitas originally meant a corporation or guild.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: a reference to a nineteenth-century law that promoted practical subjects
questions.evidence: a law passed in 1862 ... teaching agriculture and engineering.
questions.explanation: 1862 falls in the nineteenth century, and agriculture and engineering are practical subjects.

questions.q: an example of students having authority over their teachers
questions.evidence: the students themselves formed the guild, hired the teachers and could fine them.
questions.explanation: This shows students having authority. B is used twice.

questions.q: a description of how teaching was carried out when books were scarce
questions.evidence: Books were rare and expensive ... so a lecturer would read a text aloud.
questions.explanation: "Rare" = "scarce".

questions.q: an institution that combined research with teaching
questions.evidence: The University of Berlin ... organised around the principle that teaching and research should be combined.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: a reference to a large rise in student numbers following a major conflict
questions.evidence: after the Second World War ... Student numbers ... grew enormously.
questions.explanation: "Major conflict" = the Second World War.

questions.q: a mention of scientific work carried out outside universities
questions.evidence: Much of the important scientific work ... was carried out outside universities.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match. D is used twice.

questions.q: an expression of confidence that universities will continue to adapt
questions.evidence: many observers expect them to do so again.
questions.explanation: This is an expression of confidence.

lesson.title: Innovations and their effects
lesson.text: Business and technology passages often describe an innovation in one paragraph and its effects in another. Questions may ask for "the introduction of..." (the innovation) or "a consequence of..." (the effect). Make sure your paragraph contains the specific part of the story that the question asks for.
lesson.example: Paragraph C: "In 1974, barcodes were first scanned at a checkout." Paragraph D: "Scanning allowed shops to track sales precisely." Question: "a benefit of the barcode" → D, not C.

questions.q: a reason why the first self-service shop could charge less
questions.evidence: Because fewer staff were needed, prices could be lower.
questions.explanation: This is the reason.

questions.q: a reference to household appliances that changed shopping habits
questions.evidence: many households acquired refrigerators and freezers, allowing them to store food for longer.
questions.explanation: "Refrigerators and freezers" = "household appliances".

questions.q: a description of the first item ever scanned at a checkout
questions.evidence: The first product scanned ... was a packet of chewing gum.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: a benefit that barcodes provided beyond faster checkouts
questions.evidence: More importantly, they gave supermarkets detailed information about what was being sold.
questions.explanation: This benefit goes beyond speed. E is used twice.

questions.q: a reference to complaints from people who supply supermarkets
questions.evidence: farmers and suppliers, who sometimes complain that they are forced to accept low prices.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: an explanation of why customers valued cheap supermarkets in the 1930s
questions.evidence: During the economic depression ... customers who were anxious to save money.
questions.explanation: The economic depression explains why cheap prices were valued.

questions.q: a disadvantage of the traditional counter-service system
questions.evidence: Shopping was slow, required many staff, and gave customers little opportunity to compare products.
questions.explanation: These are disadvantages of counter service.

questions.q: a modern development that extends an early idea
questions.evidence: Self-service checkouts have extended Saunders' original idea.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

lesson.title: Positive vs negative information
lesson.text: Balanced passages give both benefits and criticisms. Questions often specify the evaluative direction: "a criticism of", "an advantage of", "a concern about", "an achievement". When two paragraphs discuss the same subject, check whether each is positive or negative, and match the direction of the question.
lesson.example: Two paragraphs discuss fertiliser: one praises higher yields, the other describes water pollution. Question: "an environmental drawback of fertiliser use" → the negative paragraph.

questions.q: an explanation of why traditional crops could not benefit from heavy fertiliser use
questions.evidence: the plants grew so heavy with grain that their stems bent and collapsed.
questions.explanation: This explains why traditional varieties failed with heavy fertiliser.

questions.q: a reference to an award given for work on food production
questions.evidence: Borlaug was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: a reason why the Green Revolution had limited impact in some regions
questions.evidence: Where they were not, as in many parts of Africa with less irrigation and different crops, the Green Revolution had much less effect.
questions.explanation: This gives the reason for limited impact.

questions.q: an environmental benefit of producing more food on existing land
questions.evidence: more food could be produced on existing farmland, reducing pressure to clear forests.
questions.explanation: This is positive information, whereas E's environmental points are negative.

questions.q: a social disadvantage of the new farming methods
questions.evidence: wealthier farmers were often better able to adopt them ... inequality between farmers increased.
questions.explanation: Inequality is a social disadvantage.

questions.q: a loss of variety among crops
questions.evidence: replaced many traditional local varieties, reducing the genetic diversity of crops.
questions.explanation: This describes a loss of variety. E is used twice.

questions.q: predictions of a disaster that did not happen as expected
questions.evidence: Some predicted that hundreds of millions of people would die ... That catastrophe did not occur on the scale predicted.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: a range of views about how to increase food production in future
questions.evidence: Some emphasise improved crop varieties; others stress better management of soil and water, or greater support for small farmers.
questions.explanation: This presents a range of views.

lesson.title: Experiments — design vs results vs interpretation
lesson.example: Paragraph C describes how babies listened to recordings. Paragraph D reports that they looked longer at new sounds and explains what this shows. Question: "a proposed explanation of the babies' behaviour" → D.

questions.q: a description of how the invented language was constructed
questions.evidence: nonsense syllables strung together without pauses ... certain syllables always followed one another, forming 'words'.
questions.explanation: This describes the method.

questions.q: evidence that babies could distinguish familiar from unfamiliar sequences
questions.evidence: The babies listened for longer to the less familiar combinations, showing that they could tell the two apart.
questions.explanation: This is the result, which appears in a different paragraph from the method.

questions.q: a reference to a change in babies' ability to hear differences between sounds
questions.evidence: by around ten to twelve months of age, this ability narrows.
questions.explanation: "Narrows" = "a change in ability".

questions.q: a suggested reason why live interaction helps learning
questions.evidence: The researchers proposed that social interaction increases babies' attention and motivation.
questions.explanation: This is the interpretation.

questions.q: a reference to a long-running debate about how language is acquired
questions.evidence: For a long time, it was debated whether children learn language mainly through general abilities ... or ... specialised knowledge.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: features of the way adults typically speak to babies
questions.evidence: a higher pitch, exaggerated intonation, slower speech and clearer pronunciation.
questions.explanation: These are the features of how adults speak to babies.

questions.q: a recommendation for parents based on research findings
questions.evidence: talking with babies – not simply near them – ... supports language development, and ... screens are a poor substitute.
questions.explanation: This is practical advice based on the findings.

questions.q: a comparison between babies who learned from a person and those who learned from recordings
questions.evidence: Only the babies who had interacted with a live speaker retained the ability.
questions.explanation: This compares the two groups. F is used twice.

lesson.title: Hard Matching Information — abstract question wording
lesson.text:
At Hard level, questions describe the information in abstract, general terms. For example, "an explanation of why a theory was initially dismissed" rather than "why Wegener's ideas were rejected". There are more paragraphs (often eight or nine), several contain no answer, and the passage repeatedly revisits the same subject from different angles.

Strategy:

1. Translate each abstract question into what it would look like in this passage ("theory dismissed" → Wegener rejected → look for "critics", "no mechanism").

2. Identify the function of each paragraph as you read, for example "evidence", "objection", "new technology", "consequence". Hard questions often target paragraph functions.

3. Expect the correct sentence to use none of the question's words.

questions.q: a reference to a personal criticism of the originator of a theory
questions.evidence: Some also objected that Wegener was not a trained geologist.
questions.explanation: This criticism targets the person rather than the evidence.

questions.q: a description of how rocks preserve a record of past conditions
questions.evidence: As molten rock cools, iron-rich minerals within it align with the Earth's magnetic field, preserving a record of the field's direction.
questions.explanation: This describes how rocks record past conditions.

questions.q: an explanation offered by opponents to account for evidence that seemed to support a new idea
questions.evidence: Alternative explanations for the fossil evidence were proposed, including now-vanished 'land bridges'.
questions.explanation: The land bridges were the opponents' explanation. C is used twice.

questions.q: a mention of research aims unrelated to science that led to important discoveries
questions.evidence: Improved methods of measuring the depth of the sea, many developed for military purposes, revealed ...
questions.explanation: "Military purposes" = "aims unrelated to science".

questions.q: a view that had been generally held before a radical proposal was made
questions.evidence: Most geologists assumed that continents and oceans had always occupied roughly their present positions.
questions.explanation: This was the prior consensus.

questions.q: an early suggestion about a mechanism that was later largely vindicated
questions.evidence: one of them proposed that slow currents in the hot rock deep within the Earth might carry the continents along.
questions.explanation: This early idea anticipated the later mechanism, as the "carried along" wording in G confirms. It is an abstract question that requires linking two paragraphs.

questions.q: a claim that a popular version of events is oversimplified
questions.evidence: often told as a story of a lone genius ignored ... The reality is more complicated.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: a reference to phenomena that the accepted theory was also able to explain
questions.evidence: It explained not only the fit ... but also the locations of earthquakes and volcanoes.
questions.explanation: Earthquakes and volcanoes are the "phenomena".

questions.q: evidence suggesting that some regions had once had a very different climate
questions.evidence: traces of ancient glaciers were found in places that are now tropical.
questions.explanation: This is evidence of a different past climate.

lesson.title: Tracing how interpretations change
lesson.text: In passages that describe research over several decades, the same study may be interpreted differently at different times. Questions may ask for "the original interpretation", "a later challenge" or "an alternative explanation". Mark each paragraph with its stage in the story: original study → popular interpretation → challenge → new explanation → conclusion. Many hard questions become straightforward once you know the stage of each paragraph.

questions.q: a description of techniques that helped children resist temptation
questions.evidence: children waited longer when the treat was hidden from view ... Children who distracted themselves ... tended to wait longer.
questions.explanation: These are the techniques.

questions.q: a reason why the original follow-up sample may have been unrepresentative
questions.evidence: The original participants were mostly the children of staff and students at a prestigious university, and so were far from representative.
questions.explanation: This is the reason the sample was unrepresentative.

questions.q: the effect of taking family background into account
questions.evidence: when they took account of factors such as the family's income ... the association became much smaller still.
questions.explanation: This is the effect of considering family background.

questions.q: a suggestion that not waiting may sometimes be a sensible choice
questions.evidence: eating the treat at once may be a rational decision rather than a failure of willpower.
questions.explanation: "Rational" = "sensible".

questions.q: a reference to the popular conclusion drawn from the early follow-up studies
questions.evidence: gave rise to a popular belief that the ability to delay gratification ... was a powerful predictor of later success.
questions.explanation: This is the popular conclusion.

questions.q: a statement that the original studies had a different aim from the one for which they became known
questions.evidence: The original purpose of these studies was not to predict children's futures.
questions.explanation: The paragraph contrasts the original aim with what the studies "became famous" for (C). B is used twice.

questions.q: a possible explanation for why waiting time was linked to later outcomes
questions.evidence: These same circumstances may also influence later success, which could account for part of the association.
questions.explanation: This is the possible explanation.

questions.q: support for the value of self-control from other types of research
questions.evidence: Many studies using different methods have found that people with better self-regulation tend to experience better outcomes.
questions.explanation: This support comes from other types of research.

questions.q: a reference to the proportion of original participants included in later studies
questions.evidence: only a fraction of them could be traced for the follow-up studies.
questions.explanation: "A fraction" is a proportion. D is used twice.

lesson.title: Unintended consequences and ironies
lesson.text: Hard historical passages often highlight ironies: actions taken for one reason that had an unexpected result, or theories that were wrong but led to good outcomes. Questions may describe these indirectly: "a beneficial result of a mistaken belief", "an outcome that was not the main aim of a project". Look for contrast words such as although, ironically, even though, not because... but, unintended.

questions.q: an explanation of how a new household technology worsened a problem
questions.evidence: the introduction of the flushing toilet ... made the problem worse, since the extra water caused cesspits to overflow more quickly.
questions.explanation: The flushing toilet is the household technology.

questions.q: a reference to the sale of waste for agricultural use
questions.evidence: sold the contents to farmers as fertiliser.
questions.explanation: This is a brief reference. A is used twice.

questions.q: a method used to investigate the cause of an outbreak
questions.evidence: he mapped the homes of those who had died.
questions.explanation: Mapping is the method of investigation.

questions.q: a beneficial outcome that was achieved for reasons other than those intended
questions.evidence: the sewers were built largely for the wrong reason ... they reduced cholera because they stopped waste from contaminating drinking water.
questions.explanation: This is the irony described in the lesson.

questions.q: evidence from a later epidemic supporting the effectiveness of the new system
questions.evidence: most of the deaths occurred in an area ... that had not yet been connected to the new system.
questions.explanation: The 1866 outbreak provides the evidence.

questions.q: an example of foresight in planning for future needs
questions.evidence: Bazalgette deliberately made many sewers larger than current needs required, reasoning that the population would continue to grow.
questions.explanation: This is an example of foresight.

questions.q: a reference to the unusual speed of a political decision
questions.evidence: Within weeks, Parliament passed legislation ... a remarkable speed.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: a current limitation of an old system
questions.evidence: heavy rainfall regularly causes the combined sewers ... to overflow into the Thames.
questions.explanation: This is the current limitation.

questions.q: the location where waste was released under the new scheme
questions.evidence: carry it eastwards, downstream of the city, where it was released into the river.
questions.explanation: This gives the location. E is used twice.

lesson.title: Paragraphs that contain no answers
lesson.text: In Hard sets, some paragraphs contain no answers at all, which makes elimination less reliable. Avoid choosing a letter simply because it has not yet been used. Confirm every answer with a specific sentence. If you cannot find a sentence that fits a question, reread the question's type word and look again; do not guess from topic alone.

questions.q: a reference to a counting base that survives in the measurement of time
questions.evidence: sixty ... survives in the division of hours into minutes and minutes into seconds.
questions.explanation: This is the base that survives in time measurement.

questions.q: a warning that an unfamiliar test may have affected results
questions.evidence: the experimental tasks, designed by outsiders, were unfamiliar or seemed pointless to participants.
questions.explanation: This is the warning.

questions.q: a description of a counting system that names parts of the body
questions.evidence: people count by touching or naming parts of the body in a fixed order.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: a claim that exact reasoning about large numbers is partly a cultural achievement
questions.evidence: our ability to reason precisely about large numbers is not simply an innate gift but, in part, an invention of human culture.
questions.explanation: "Invention of human culture" = "a cultural achievement".

questions.q: evidence from people who communicate using gestures invented within their families
questions.evidence: develop their own systems of gestures, known as home signs, to communicate with their families.
questions.explanation: This is the evidence from home-sign users.

questions.q: a description of the typical order in which children learn number meanings
questions.evidence: Children typically learn the meaning of 'one', then 'two', then 'three'.
questions.explanation: This describes the typical order.

questions.q: results showing accurate performance with very small numbers only
questions.evidence: They performed accurately with two or three objects, but with larger numbers their responses became approximate.
questions.explanation: G reports a similar pattern, but it describes gestures used in communication, not the results of a test. The question's "results showing ... performance" fits D's experiment best.

questions.q: an example from a European language of a base other than ten
questions.evidence: French, for example, expresses eighty as 'four twenties'.
questions.explanation: This is an example of base twenty in a European language. B is used twice.

lesson.title: Distinguishing scientific discovery, technical development and economic change
lesson.text: Technology histories move through different kinds of events: a scientific discovery (a phenomenon is observed), a technical development (a practical device is made), and an economic or social change (cost falls, use spreads). Questions often specify one kind. For example, "the first practical application" is not the same as "the discovery of the effect". Label each paragraph accordingly.

questions.q: the first observation of a scientific effect
questions.evidence: observed that shining light on certain materials ... produced a small electric current.
questions.explanation: This is the scientific discovery. C is the first practical cell, a technical development, which makes it a trap.

questions.q: an example of an early media prediction that proved too optimistic
questions.evidence: one predicted that it might eventually provide almost limitless energy. The reality was more modest.
questions.explanation: This is the over-optimistic media prediction.

questions.q: a reason why an early market was willing to pay high prices
questions.evidence: cost was less important than weight and reliability.
questions.explanation: This explains why satellites could justify high prices.

questions.q: a relationship between the growth of production and the fall in prices
questions.evidence: each doubling of the total amount of solar capacity manufactured has been associated with a fall of roughly a fifth in the price.
questions.explanation: This is the relationship between production and price.

questions.q: a reference to government support that was later reduced
questions.evidence: when oil prices fell again in the 1980s, much of this support was withdrawn.
questions.explanation: "Withdrawn" = "reduced".

questions.q: a remaining challenge in storing energy over long periods
questions.evidence: storing large amounts of energy for long periods ... remains difficult and expensive.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: a reference to an explanation of an effect that came much later than its discovery
questions.evidence: A satisfactory explanation ... had to wait for developments in physics in the early twentieth century.
questions.explanation: B is used twice.

questions.q: examples of uses in isolated locations
questions.evidence: lighthouses, telecommunications equipment in deserts.
questions.explanation: These are isolated locations. E is used twice.

questions.q: a suggestion that a strategy might be applied to other fields
questions.evidence: Whether similar approaches can be used to accelerate other technologies is a question of considerable importance.
questions.explanation: This suggests applying the strategy elsewhere.

lesson.title: Final review — the complete method

questions.q: an explanation of why the toads failed to reduce the pests
questions.evidence: The beetles lived mainly in the upper parts of the cane plants, while the toads, which cannot climb well, hunted on the ground.
questions.explanation: This explains the failure.

questions.q: a process by which the invasion became faster over time
questions.evidence: when they bred with one another, their offspring inherited these traits, so that the invasion accelerated.
questions.explanation: This is the process that made the invasion faster.

questions.q: evidence that training can improve the survival of a native species
questions.evidence: Trials have shown that trained quolls survive longer after toads arrive than untrained ones.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: a reference to changes in regulations resulting from this case
questions.evidence: it has influenced the much stricter rules that now govern such introductions.
questions.explanation: "Stricter rules" = "changes in regulations".

questions.q: a point on which people with differing views agree
questions.evidence: Both groups agree, however, that prevention ... is far cheaper and more effective.
questions.explanation: This is the point of agreement.

questions.q: the reason the toads were originally introduced
questions.evidence: intended to control beetles whose larvae were damaging the roots of sugar cane.
questions.explanation: This is the original reason.

questions.q: physical changes in native animals that may reduce the harm caused by toads
questions.evidence: evolved smaller mouths that make it harder to swallow large toads.
questions.explanation: This is a physical change. The birds' learned behaviour is behavioural, not physical, but the snakes' change satisfies the question.

questions.q: a description of the mechanism by which toads harm predators
questions.evidence: Cane toads produce a powerful toxin in glands behind their heads ... [predators] attack and eat the toads and are poisoned.
questions.explanation: This describes the mechanism.

questions.q: a reference to methods that have reduced toad numbers only in limited areas
questions.evidence: None of these methods has halted the invasion ... although some may reduce toad numbers locally.
questions.explanation: "Locally" = "only in limited areas". F is used twice.

lesson.title: Use the first sentence
lesson.text: In easy passages, the first sentence of each paragraph usually tells you the topic directly. Read it carefully, then skim the rest of the paragraph to confirm. If the rest of the paragraph develops the same idea, the first sentence is your main idea.
lesson.example: "The new bridge brought many benefits to the town. Journeys became shorter, trade increased, and..." → main idea: benefits of the new bridge.

questions.q: Paragraph A
questions.evidence: they were often symbols of high rank. Only kings, nobles and religious leaders were entitled ...
questions.explanation: The paragraph's main point is that umbrellas were a status symbol.

questions.q: Paragraph B
questions.evidence: The Chinese are usually credited with developing umbrellas that could protect against rain.
questions.explanation: The whole paragraph concerns early waterproof umbrellas in Asia.

questions.q: Paragraph C
questions.evidence: A man carrying an umbrella, however, was widely regarded as weak or unmanly.
questions.explanation: The contrast word "however" introduces the main point about men. The first sentence introduces the European context.

questions.q: Paragraph D
questions.evidence: Jonas Hanway ... carried an umbrella in public for around thirty years ... by the end of the century the umbrella had become an acceptable item for men.
questions.explanation: Hanway made umbrellas acceptable. Heading vii is a detail trap: carriage drivers are mentioned only briefly, and the paragraph says nothing about their role in sales.

questions.q: Paragraph E
questions.evidence: A major improvement came in 1852 ... steel ribs ... compact folding umbrellas and waterproof synthetic fabrics.
questions.explanation: The paragraph covers improvements in both materials and design.

questions.q: Paragraph F
questions.evidence: the basic design has changed surprisingly little ... none of these has replaced the traditional form.
questions.explanation: This matches "enduring design despite new ideas". Heading ii contradicts the paragraph, since nothing has replaced the umbrella.

lesson.title: Avoid headings that cover only one example
lesson.text: A paragraph often gives a general idea followed by several examples. A heading that names only one of those examples is too narrow. Choose the heading that covers the general idea behind them.
lesson.example: Paragraph: "Parks improve physical health. People walk, run and play sports there, and children have space to exercise." Heading "A place for children to play" is too narrow; "Benefits for physical health" is correct.

questions.q: Paragraph A
questions.evidence: As industrial cities grew ... Reformers began to argue that public parks were a necessity.
questions.explanation: The paragraph explains why industrial cities needed parks.

questions.q: Paragraph B
questions.evidence: One of the most influential parks ... The park's success inspired similar projects.
questions.explanation: Central Park was a landmark design that influenced others.

questions.q: Paragraph C
questions.evidence: take more physical exercise ... lower levels of stress and improved mood.
questions.explanation: The paragraph covers both physical and mental benefits.

questions.q: Paragraph D
questions.evidence: absorb rainwater ... provide shade ... give shelter to birds.
questions.explanation: Heading iv (wildlife) covers only one example, so it is too narrow. Heading viii covers flooding, temperature and wildlife.

questions.q: Paragraph E
questions.evidence: parks bring people together.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: Paragraph F
questions.evidence: Maintaining parks, however, is expensive ... parks are often among the first services to be cut.
questions.explanation: The main idea is the cost of maintenance. Heading ix is a detail: feeling unsafe is one consequence of neglect. Heading vii concerns building new parks, not maintaining existing ones.

lesson.title: Process paragraphs vs history paragraphs vs use paragraphs
lesson.text: In passages about products, paragraphs usually have different functions: how it is made, its history, its uses, its problems. Headings reflect these functions. Identify the function of each paragraph before choosing a heading, and watch for headings that mention the right subject but the wrong function (for example, "the history of beekeeping" for a paragraph about how bees make honey).

questions.q: Paragraph A
questions.evidence: enzymes ... break down the complex sugars ... evaporating much of its water.
questions.explanation: This is a process paragraph about how nectar becomes honey.

questions.q: Paragraph B
questions.evidence: Humans have collected honey for thousands of years ... Later, people began to keep bees.
questions.explanation: This is a history paragraph. Heading viii concerns modern practical advice, which the paragraph does not give.

questions.q: Paragraph C
questions.evidence: Honey has a remarkable ability to resist decay ... can last almost indefinitely.
questions.explanation: Heading iv is a detail trap: tombs are only an example, and they are not specifically Egyptian in this paragraph.

questions.q: Paragraph D
questions.evidence: Ancient doctors ... applied it to wounds ... Some hospitals today use ... medical honey.
questions.explanation: The paragraph covers both old and new medical uses.

questions.q: Paragraph E
questions.evidence: Bee colonies ... have suffered from diseases ... some honey ... mixed with cheaper sugar syrups.
questions.explanation: Threats to colonies affect supply, and adulteration affects quality.

lesson.title: Explanation paragraphs
lesson.text: In science passages, several paragraphs may explain the same phenomenon from different angles: why it happens, what conditions are needed, a special case, how it was first explained. Headings will differ in exactly these ways. Ask of each paragraph: Is it explaining the cause, the conditions, a variation, or the history of the explanation?

questions.q: Paragraph A
questions.evidence: many cultures have explained them through myths.
questions.explanation: The paragraph is about myths and stories.

questions.q: Paragraph B
questions.evidence: A scientific explanation began to emerge ... Together, these discoveries explained how rainbows are formed.
questions.explanation: This paragraph gives the history of the explanation. Heading ix is too narrow: it names Newton, but the paragraph covers Descartes too and concerns only the rainbow.

questions.q: Paragraph C
questions.evidence: As the light passes from air into water, it bends ... reflected off the back of the raindrop.
questions.explanation: This paragraph explains the cause.

questions.q: Paragraph D
questions.evidence: Seeing a rainbow requires particular conditions.
questions.explanation: This paragraph describes the conditions.

questions.q: Paragraph E
questions.evidence: This double rainbow is caused by light reflecting twice ... reverses the order of the colours.
questions.explanation: The paragraph covers both the cause and the appearance of the second bow.

questions.q: Paragraph F
questions.evidence: no two people see exactly the same rainbow ... not an object located in a particular place.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.
